title: Climbing Stairs
description: Ways to reach step n taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Fibonacci-shaped DP: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). O(1) space with rolling variables.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me play it back: I'm standing at the bottom of `n` stairs. At every move I can take exactly 1 step or 2 steps. I want to count the number of distinct sequences of moves that land me on step `n`."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Range of `n` — fits in a 32-bit int? Could it be 0?
• Is `n=0` a valid input — and if so, is the answer 1 (the empty sequence) or 0?
• Are 1-then-2 and 2-then-1 counted as different sequences? (They should be — it's ordered.)
• Return value — just the count, or also the sequences themselves?
sections.why: The `n=0` and ordering questions look pedantic but they pin down the base case. If 1-2 and 2-1 are the *same*, this becomes a partition-counting problem with a totally different recurrence. And `n=0 → 1` is what makes `ways(2) = ways(1) + ways(0) = 1 + 1 = 2` work cleanly — without it the seed gets ugly.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(2^n) solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The obvious recursive version is: `ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)`, with `ways(0) = ways(1) = 1`. At every step you either took a 1 or a 2; sum the two subtrees. Plain recursion is O(2^n) time because `ways(n-1)` and `ways(n-2)` re-derive overlapping subproblems — `ways(n-3)` gets computed in both branches, `ways(n-4)` four times, and so on. Same shape as the naive Fibonacci recursion."
sections.why: Two reasons to name it. (1) Most interviewers want to see you reach for recursion first — it's the natural decomposition of 'last move was 1 or 2'. (2) The overlap is the whole reason DP applies. Once you say 'I'm recomputing the same subtree', memoization → tabulation → rolling-pair is a straight line, and it's clear *why* each step helps.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to bottom-up DP with rolling variables?
sections.say: "This is a 1D DP problem. The recurrence is the load-bearing piece: to land on step `n`, the last move was either a 1 (so I was on step `n-1`) or a 2 (so I was on step `n-2`). Those two subproblems are disjoint and cover every sequence, so `ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)` — straight Fibonacci. Once I see that each `dp[i]` only reads `dp[i-1]` and `dp[i-2]`, the array is overkill: I keep two rolling scalars `prev2` and `prev1`, slide them forward in a loop, and the answer is the final `prev1`. Time O(n), space O(1)."
sections.why: Naming the recurrence in plain language — 'last move was 1 or 2, so sum the two predecessors' — is the move. Anyone can say 'this is Fibonacci'; the win is *deriving* it from the decision at each step. The rolling-vars observation comes from inspecting the recurrence's read-window: if the recurrence only reaches back `k` cells, you only need `k` rolling vars.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — the canonical n=5, the n=1 base case, and a slightly larger n=7 to confirm the Fibonacci pattern keeps holding.

examples.note: Canonical case — produces the familiar Fibonacci sequence 1,1,2,3,5,8.
examples.trace:
init: prev2=ways(0)=1, prev1=ways(1)=1
i=2: curr = prev1+prev2 = 1+1 = 2. roll → prev2=1, prev1=2. dp so far [1,1,2]
i=3: curr = 2+1 = 3. roll → prev2=2, prev1=3. dp [1,1,2,3]
i=4: curr = 3+2 = 5. roll → prev2=3, prev1=5. dp [1,1,2,3,5]
i=5: curr = 5+3 = 8. roll → prev2=5, prev1=8. dp [1,1,2,3,5,8]
return prev1 = 8

examples.note: Base case — the early return fires before the loop runs.
Larger — confirms the rolling-pair carries the Fibonacci forward without divergence.
examples.trace:
init: prev2=1, prev1=1
i=2: curr=2, roll → (1,2)
i=3: curr=3, roll → (2,3)
i=4: curr=5, roll → (3,5)
i=5: curr=8, roll → (5,8)
i=6: curr=13, roll → (8,13)
i=7: curr=21, roll → (13,21)
return 21

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the one bug this problem rewards: the roll order. If you assign `prev1 = curr` *before* `prev2 = prev1`, you overwrite `prev1` with `curr` and then copy that same `curr` into `prev2` — both rails collapse and you compute the wrong sequence. The n=1 trace also defends the base case: without `ways(0) = 1`, the loop's first iteration would start from the wrong seed.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• `n = 0` — depends on the convention you pick in clarification. Either return 1 (the empty sequence) or guard against it explicitly.
• `n = 1` and `n = 2` — both should return 1 and 2 respectively; the early return covers `n ≤ 1` and the loop body covers `n = 2` cleanly.
• Very large `n` (e.g. 80+) — the answer overflows a regular JS Number's safe integer range around `n ≈ 78`. If the spec needs exact arithmetic beyond that, switch the rolling vars to BigInt.
• Negative `n` — almost certainly invalid; either throw or treat as 0 depending on the contract."
sections.why: The integer-overflow call-out is the senior signal here. Most candidates blow past it because the Fibonacci numbers feel benign; pointing out that JS Numbers lose precision around `2^53` (which Fibonacci hits surprisingly fast) shows you actually thought about the data type, not just the algorithm. The interviewer either nods or says 'assume `n ≤ 45`' — both are fine outcomes.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — single pass from `i = 2` to `n`, constant work per iteration (one add, two assignments). Space is O(1) — just the two rolling scalars `prev2` and `prev1`, no array allocation.

The naive recursive version was O(2^n) time because of the overlapping-subproblems blow-up; memoization brings it to O(n) time / O(n) space; tabulation keeps O(n) / O(n); rolling pair drops space to O(1). Same answer, three different memory profiles.

If you wanted to extend to 'you can step 1, 2, or 3 at a time', the recurrence becomes `ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) + ways(n-3)` (a tribonacci) and you'd need three rolling vars. Same template, different look-back depth."
sections.why: Walking the 2^n → n → 1 progression in space is the right way to defend the rolling-vars choice — the interviewer sees you understand why DP works (overlapping subproblems) and why you can compress (limited look-back). The tribonacci extension proves you see the template as 'k-step Fibonacci' rather than memorizing this one problem; that same shape recurs in House Robber, Min Cost Climbing Stairs, and Decode Ways.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the canonical Fibonacci-shape DP one statement at a time. The state panel shows the rolling pair (prev2, prev1) plus a synthetic dp array so you can see the table fill.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — n=${n}`, state: { n } };
yield { line: 2, label: `n=${n} <= 1 — return 1`, state: { n, returns: 1 } };
yield { line: 4, label: 'seed bases: prev2=ways(0)=1, prev1=ways(1)=1', state: { n, prev2, prev1, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 6, label: `outer step: i=${i} — compute ways(${i})`, state: { n, i, prev2, prev1, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 7, label: `curr = prev1 + prev2 = ${prev1} + ${prev2} = ${curr}`, state: { n, i, prev2, prev1, curr, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 9, label: `roll: prev2 = prev1 = ${prev2}`, state: { n, i, prev2, prev1, curr, dp: [...dp] } };
yield { line: 10, label: `roll: prev1 = curr = ${prev1} — dp[${i}]=${curr} filled`, state: { n, i, prev2, prev1, dp: [...dp], lastFilled: i } };
yield { line: 12, label: `return prev1 = ${prev1}`, state: { n, prev2, prev1, dp: [...dp], returns: prev1 } };

reference.approach: Bottom-up Fibonacci recurrence with two rolling scalars
notes: Recurrence: to land on step i you came from i-1 (1 step) or i-2 (2 steps), so ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2).
Base cases: ways(0) = 1 (one way: stay) and ways(1) = 1. Both seed prev2 and prev1.
Only the last two values matter — use two rolling scalars and drop space to O(1).
reference.crux: The last move was a 1-step or a 2-step, so ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) — plain Fibonacci; keep two rolling scalars for O(1) space.
cruxDistractors: Recurse ways(n)=ways(n-1)+ways(n-2) with no memo — recomputes the same subtrees exponentially.
Count arrangements directly: with k two-steps there are C(n-k, k) orderings, so sum the binomials over k.
Each new step doubles the choices, so the answer is 2^(n-1) ways to reach step n.

alternates.label: DP array (O(n) space)
alternates.when: Reach for this as the 'teaching step' before the rolling-pair optimization: it makes the Fibonacci table explicit and is easier to explain in an interview when you're building up to the O(1)-space version. Some interviewers prefer seeing the table first.
notes: Identical recurrence to the rolling-pair version — just stores every Fibonacci value instead of only the last two.
The full dp array is a useful teaching aid: you can point to dp[i] and explain 'this is the number of ways to reach step i' without describing the rolling state.
Transition to O(1) space: notice dp[i] reads only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2] — two rolling scalars are sufficient.

alternates.label: Top-down memoization (O(n) / O(n))
alternates.when: Reach for this when the interviewer asks for the recursive formulation first, or you want to show the memoization pattern before deriving the bottom-up table. Natural to write if you're already thinking of the recursion.
notes: Each subproblem dp(k) is computed once; subsequent calls return from memo in O(1).
Recursion depth is O(n) — hits JS's call stack limit around n≈10000; prefer the iterative version for large n.
The three versions (memo → table → rolling-pair) form the canonical DP optimization ladder: O(2^n) → O(n)/O(n) → O(n)/O(1).

questions.q: The recurrence for climbing n stairs (1 or 2 at a time) is:
options: ways(n) = ways(n-1) * 2
ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)
ways(n) = n!
ways(n) = 2^n
questions.explain: Every path to step n ends with either a 1-step (from n-1) or a 2-step (from n-2), so the two disjoint counts add — that is the `prev1 + prev2` in the loop.

questions.q: What sequence do the dp values follow?
options: Powers of two
Fibonacci
Triangular numbers
Catalan numbers
questions.explain: Seeded 1, 1 and each term the sum of the previous two, the loop walks 1,1,2,3,5,8 — which is why `climbStairs(5)` is 8. Powers of two would need every step to be an independent binary choice; here the two branches merge into one count.

options: The recurrence is associative, so any two dp values can be combined later — no need to keep them all
Only the last two dp values are ever read
Numeric scalars use 8 bytes regardless of n, so the total is constant
Because the answer fits in a single 64-bit double for all n we care about
questions.explain: `curr = prev1 + prev2` reaches back exactly two cells, so nothing older than i-2 is ever read again and a dp array would just be a log. The 8-bytes-per-scalar argument is about an array's element SIZE, but what grows with n is its length.

questions.q: Time complexity of the iterative bottom-up version?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
questions.explain: A single loop from i=2 to n with constant work per step is O(n).

questions.q: WHY is the recurrence ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)?
options: Because n is split in half each time
Because the last move was either a 1-step (from n-1) or a 2-step (from n-2), and those cases are disjoint
Because every step doubles the options
It is an arbitrary pattern that happens to work
questions.explain: Every path to step n ends with exactly one of two moves; summing the disjoint counts of ways to reach n-1 and n-2 covers all paths exactly once.

questions.q: Why is naive recursion ways(n)=ways(n-1)+ways(n-2) O(2^n)?
options: Each recursive call doubles the stack frame size, so total memory grows as 2^n
The same subproblems (e.g. ways(n-3)) are recomputed in many branches — overlapping subproblems
Each call evaluates `ways(n-1)` and `ways(n-2)` in parallel, and the join cost compounds exponentially
Because the answer itself is roughly 2^n, and any algorithm that produces an exponential output must take exponential time
questions.explain: Without memoization the recursion tree re-derives identical subtrees repeatedly; caching them collapses it to O(n).

questions.q: Why does the roll assign `prev2 = prev1` BEFORE `prev1 = curr`?
options: Because prev1 is declared first, so JS hoisting requires the matching assignment order
Reversing the order overwrites prev1 first, so prev2 gets curr and both rails collapse to the wrong value
Otherwise the loop body's last assignment short-circuits via const re-binding
To keep the recurrence symmetric with the n-2 base case
questions.explain: prev2 must capture the OLD prev1; if prev1 is updated first, the old value is lost and the sequence diverges.

questions.q: If each move could be 1, 2, or 3 stairs, the recurrence becomes:
options: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) + ways(n-3)
ways(n) = ways(n-1) * 3
ways(n) = ways(n-3)
ways(n) = 3^n
questions.explain: The last move is now one of three sizes, so sum the three disjoint predecessors (tribonacci) — same template, deeper look-back.

L3.prompt: Write `climbStairs(n)` returning the number of ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Use O(1) space. Log `climbStairs(5)`.
hints: Recurrence is Fibonacci: ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2).
